cases.description: Plain in-order delivery. No overlap, no ambiguity.
cases.title: Three contiguous segments

cases.description: Segments arrive 3, 1, 2. Reordering alone is not ambiguity.
cases.title: Three segments, reordered

cases.description: A segment is retransmitted byte for byte.
cases.title: Exact retransmission

cases.description: Lost data is resent as larger, differently aligned segments (identical bytes). Honest TCP stacks do this routinely; a tap must not call it an attack.
cases.title: Retransmission with different segmentation

cases.description: Data beyond a hole is buffered until the missing segment arrives.
cases.title: Hole filled later

cases.description: Single-byte segments: every frame is padded to the Ethernet minimum, so a parser that trusts the frame length instead of the IP length would append zero bytes.
cases.title: One-byte segments

cases.description: The 32-bit sequence number wraps in the middle of the stream.
cases.title: Sequence wrap, in order

cases.description: A segment that lies just past the 32-bit wrap arrives before the bytes that precede it. A naive `seq < next_expected` test mistakes it for an old duplicate and drops it.
cases.title: Sequence wrap, out of order

cases.description: The same sequence range is sent twice with different bytes: the tap and the endpoint can keep different copies.
cases.title: Same range, different bytes

cases.description: First and last copies agree but a middle copy differs: 'first' and 'last' reassemble the same stream although the flow is ambiguous.
cases.title: A, B, A on the same range (delivered)

cases.description: As above, with the range buffered beyond a hole.
cases.title: A, B, A on the same range (buffered)

cases.description: A overlaps B, B overlaps C, all with different bytes, buffered beyond a hole.
cases.title: Chain of three overlapping segments

cases.description: A large segment arrives after three small segments it contradicts.
cases.title: One large segment over three small ones

cases.description: A large segment arrives first and three smaller segments contradict parts of it.
cases.title: Large segment, then small contradictions

cases.description: A conflicting segment straddles the 2**32 boundary after the original data was delivered.
cases.title: Conflict spanning the sequence wrap (delivered)

cases.description: As above, with both copies buffered beyond a hole.
cases.title: Conflict spanning the sequence wrap (buffered)

cases.description: The conflicting copy arrives before the server has acknowledged the range.
cases.title: Conflicting retransmission before the ACK

cases.description: RFC 1122 lets a keep-alive probe carry one garbage octet at the last sequence number already acknowledged. It contradicts real data, so it is flagged, but it is the one benign-looking source of a conflict the corpus knows about.
cases.title: Keep-alive probe with a garbage octet

cases.description: A decoy segment with a wrong checksum precedes the real one. Endpoints discard it; a tap that does not verify checksums reassembles the decoy bytes.
cases.title: Decoy with a bad TCP checksum

cases.description: A segment with a wrong checksum covers a range no valid segment ever carries. The endpoint never receives it and stalls at the hole; a checksum-blind tap splices the decoy into the stream and, because nothing overlaps, sees no conflict at all.
cases.title: Decoy with a bad checksum fills a hole

cases.description: The SYN carries bytes that a later segment contradicts. Linux without TCP Fast Open ignores SYN payload; a tap that counts it disagrees with the endpoint.
cases.title: Payload on the SYN

cases.description: Bytes are sent past the stream's FIN. The application sees EOF at the FIN.
cases.title: Payload beyond the FIN

cases.description: The stream is closed at two different offsets.
cases.title: Two FINs at different offsets

cases.description: One segment travels as two IP fragments. Endpoints reassemble them; a tap that does not reassemble IP fragments never sees the bytes.
cases.title: Segment split into IPv4 fragments

cases.description: The tap joined mid-connection: the stream start has to be inferred.
cases.title: Capture without the handshake

cases.description: A segment begins three bytes before the first data byte; the endpoint trims those bytes.
cases.title: Segment starting before the stream

cases.description: Q starts inside P and runs past its end. The bytes before P and P itself reach the endpoint in order and are ACKed before Q arrives, so Q tries to rewrite data the application may already have.

cases.description: Q starts inside P and runs past its end. P then Q arrive while the stream prefix is still missing; the prefix arrives last.
cases.title: Overlap, tail, buffered beyond a hole (P first)

cases.description: Q starts inside P and runs past its end. Same as the P-first case with the arrival order of P and Q swapped.

policy_docs.first: Earliest-captured claim wins every byte (retransmitted data never replaces what was seen).
policy_docs.last: Latest-captured claim wins every byte (a naive 'overwrite on retransmit' tap).
policy_docs.linux: Model of the Linux receive path: lowest start offset wins, then the longer claim, then the earlier capture; bytes already delivered in order are frozen; payload on a SYN is ignored (no Fast Open).  Checked against a live kernel by `packet-forge kernel-verify`.
policy_docs.lowseq: Claim with the lowest start offset wins; ties go to the earlier capture.
